people.name: Augustus
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Divi filius Augustus (born Gaius Octavius)
people.summary: Founder of the Principate. Great-nephew and adopted son of Julius Caesar, he won the civil wars at Actium (31 BC) and then, through the settlements of 27 and 23 BC, built a monarchy disguised as a restored Republic that lasted, in its essentials, for three centuries.
people.detail: His power rested on control of the armies and of Egypt, on tribunicia potestas and imperium maius, and on an auctoritas cultivated through building (he claimed to have found Rome brick and left it marble), religion, moral legislation and an all-pervasive visual programme. He doubled the size of the empire, created a standing professional army with fixed terms and a military treasury, and organised Rome's city administration. His long search for an heir (Marcellus, Agrippa, Gaius and Lucius, finally Tiberius) dominated his reign. Sources: his own Res Gestae, Suetonius's Life, Dio books 51-56, Velleius (adulatory), Tacitus Annals 1 (hostile). Modern views range from Syme's ruthless faction-leader to Zanker's master of images.
people.death: natural causes at Nola, 19 August AD 14; deified 17 September

people.name: Livia

roles.t: Augusta and priestess of Divus Augustus

people.summary: Wife of Augustus for 52 years and mother of Tiberius and Drusus by her first husband Tiberius Claudius Nero. The most influential woman of the early Principate, granted sacrosanctity (35 BC) and adopted into the Julian family as Julia Augusta by Augustus's will.
people.detail: Tacitus and Dio cast her as a poisoner who cleared the way for Tiberius by eliminating Marcellus, Gaius, Lucius, Postumus and even Augustus; modern scholars largely reject these charges, seeing a powerful patron and adviser. She managed huge estates and a household of over a thousand slaves and freedmen known from the columbarium of her staff. Her villa at Prima Porta produced the garden frescoes and the Augustus of Prima Porta. Claudius deified her in 42.

people.name: Agrippa

roles.t: Holder of tribunicia potestas and imperium maius

people.summary: Augustus's lifelong friend, admiral and right-hand man, victor of Naulochus and Actium, builder of the Pantheon, the Aqua Virgo and the Baths of Agrippa, husband of Julia and father of Gaius, Lucius, Agrippina the Elder and Agrippa Postumus.
people.detail: Of obscure equestrian family, he declined triumphs to avoid overshadowing Augustus. In the principate he governed the East (23-21, 16-13 BC), ended the Cantabrian war (19 BC) and settled the Bosporus (14 BC). He compiled a world map (orbis pictus) displayed in the Porticus Vipsania, used by Pliny. His powers from 18 BC made him effectively co-regent and designated successor.

people.name: Julia the Elder
people.summary: Augustus's only child, married successively to Marcellus, Agrippa (five children) and Tiberius, and the instrument of his dynastic policy. Exiled to Pandateria in 2 BC for adultery and possibly conspiracy; she died at Rhegium soon after her father.
people.death: starvation or neglect at Rhegium, AD 14

people.name: Marcellus
people.summary: Augustus's nephew and first son-in-law, married to Julia in 25 BC and widely seen as heir; his early death at 19 was lamented by Virgil in Aeneid 6 and commemorated by the Theatre of Marcellus.

people.name: Maecenas

roles.t: Augustus's agent in Rome and Italy

people.summary: Etruscan-born equestrian friend and agent of Augustus who never held office, managing Rome in his absences and patronising Virgil, Horace and Propertius, so that his name became a byword for literary patronage.
people.detail: His influence waned after 23 BC, perhaps because of his wife Terentia's link to the Murena conspiracy. Seneca mocked his effeminate prose style and luxury. His gardens on the Esquiline included the 'auditorium of Maecenas'. He left his estate to Augustus.

people.name: Drusus the Elder
people.summary: Younger son of Livia and brother of Tiberius, conqueror of Raetia (15 BC) and the first Roman general to reach the Elbe (9 BC). Popular and reputedly republican in sympathy, he died after a riding accident in Germany; his sons were Germanicus and Claudius.
people.death: complications after a fall from his horse in Germany, 9 BC

people.name: Gaius Caesar
people.summary: Eldest son of Agrippa and Julia, adopted by Augustus in 17 BC and groomed as heir. He met the Parthian king on the Euphrates in AD 2, was wounded at Artagira in Armenia, and died at Limyra.
people.death: after a wound received at Artagira, at Limyra, 21 February AD 4

people.name: Lucius Caesar
people.summary: Younger son of Agrippa and Julia, adopted by Augustus with his brother; he died suddenly at Massilia on his way to Spain, honoured with the cenotaph decrees of Pisa.

people.name: Agrippa Postumus
people.fullName: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa Postumus (Agrippa Julius Caesar)
people.summary: Posthumous son of Agrippa, adopted by Augustus in AD 4 alongside Tiberius but disowned and exiled to Planasia in AD 7 for his violent temper; killed immediately after Augustus's death.

people.name: Julia the Younger
people.summary: Granddaughter of Augustus, wife of Lucius Aemilius Paullus; exiled to the island of Trimerus in AD 8 for adultery with Decimus Silanus, the same year as Ovid's banishment, and died there twenty years later.

people.name: Tiberius
people.fullName: Tiberius Julius Caesar Augustus (born Tiberius Claudius Nero)

roles.t: Commander in the Alps, Illyricum and Germany

people.summary: Son of Livia and stepson of Augustus, the greatest general of his generation (Raetia, Pannonia, Germany, the Illyrian revolt), adopted in AD 4 and emperor from 14 to 37. His reign was fiscally prudent and militarily cautious but darkened by treason trials, the ascendancy of Sejanus and his withdrawal to Capri.
people.detail: Tacitus's portrait of a dissembling tyrant whose true nature emerged as restraints fell away has shaped his image; Velleius, who served under him, gives the opposite view. Modern historians (Levick, Seager) stress his genuine respect for senatorial forms, his reluctance and his isolation. He left 2,700 million sesterces in the treasury.
people.death: at Misenum, 16 March 37, possibly smothered by Macro

people.name: Germanicus

roles.t: Commander in the East with imperium maius

people.summary: Son of Drusus the Elder, adopted by Tiberius in AD 4, husband of Augustus's granddaughter Agrippina and father of Caligula. Hugely popular, he quelled the Rhine mutiny of 14, campaigned in Germany (14-16), and died in Antioch convinced he had been poisoned by Piso.
people.detail: He also wrote poetry, including a Latin version of Aratus's Phaenomena that survives. His death became the founding grievance of his family's feud with Tiberius. Tacitus idealises him, though his campaigns achieved little at great cost.
people.death: illness, alleged poisoning, near Antioch, 10 October AD 19

people.name: Agrippina the Elder
people.summary: Daughter of Agrippa and Julia, wife of Germanicus and mother of nine children including Caligula and Agrippina the Younger. Proud of her Augustan blood, she saved the Rhine bridge in 15, carried Germanicus's ashes to Rome, and was exiled by Tiberius to Pandateria, where she starved to death.

people.name: Drusus the Younger
people.summary: Tiberius's only son, who suppressed the Pannonian mutiny of 14 and was designated successor after Germanicus's death; poisoned, according to later revelations, by his wife Livilla and Sejanus.

people.name: Antonia Minor
people.summary: Daughter of Mark Antony and Octavia, widow of Drusus the Elder and mother of Germanicus, Livilla and Claudius. Respected for her virtue and influence, she warned Tiberius of Sejanus's plot in 31.
people.death: in 37, perhaps by suicide or poison under Caligula

people.name: Sejanus
people.summary: Equestrian from Volsinii who, as praetorian prefect, concentrated the guard in one camp, became Tiberius's indispensable minister after the emperor withdrew to Capri, and destroyed Agrippina's family before being himself destroyed in October 31.
people.detail: Whether he aimed at the throne, at regency for a Julio-Claudian minor, or simply at survival is disputed. The 'Sejanus affair' generated a wave of prosecutions and a lasting literary topos (Juvenal 10, Ben Jonson's Sejanus).

people.name: Livilla
people.summary: Sister of Germanicus and Claudius, wife of Drusus the Younger, alleged lover of Sejanus and accomplice in poisoning her husband; she died after the revelations of 31, starved by her mother Antonia according to Dio.

people.name: Macro
people.summary: Praetorian prefect who executed Sejanus's downfall in 31, allegedly smothered the dying Tiberius, and backed Caligula's accession, only to be forced to suicide by him in 38.

people.name: Tiberius Gemellus
people.summary: Grandson of Tiberius and co-heir in his will, set aside by the Senate in favour of Caligula, who adopted him and then forced him to kill himself, probably late in 37.

people.name: Caligula
people.summary: Son of Germanicus and Agrippina, nicknamed 'Little Boot' by the Rhine soldiers. After a popular start his reign became notorious for cruelty, extravagance and demands for divine honours; he was murdered by praetorian officers after less than four years.
people.detail: The sources (Seneca, Philo, Suetonius, Dio) are uniformly hostile and contain much anecdote (the horse Incitatus as consul, the seashells). Modern accounts (Barrett, Winterling) present an autocrat who exposed the hypocrisy of the Augustan system by humiliating the Senate openly, rather than a madman.

people.name: Drusilla
people.summary: Favourite sister of Caligula, named his heir during his illness of 37, and after her death the first Roman woman deified (as Diva Drusilla).

people.name: Cassius Chaerea
people.summary: Praetorian tribune and veteran of the Rhine mutiny of 14 who, repeatedly mocked by Caligula with effeminate watchwords, led his assassination; Claudius had him executed.

people.name: Claudius
people.summary: Son of Drusus the Elder, kept from public life by his disabilities, made emperor by the praetorians in 41. His reign saw the conquest of Britain, annexations of Mauretania, Lycia and Thrace, the harbour at Portus, liberal grants of citizenship and the rise of freedman secretaries such as Narcissus and Pallas.
people.detail: A learned antiquarian, he wrote histories of the Etruscans and Carthaginians (lost) and tried to add three letters to the Latin alphabet. Ancient writers depict him as dominated by wives and freedmen; modern assessments (Levick, Osgood) credit him with energetic centralising administration. His speech on Gallic senators survives on the Lyon Tablet.

people.name: Messalina
people.summary: Third wife of Claudius and mother of Britannicus and Octavia, depicted by Tacitus and Juvenal as insatiable and murderous; executed after her public 'marriage' to Gaius Silius in 48.
people.death: executed in the Gardens of Lucullus, 48

people.name: Narcissus
people.summary: Freedman secretary of Claudius, immensely rich and powerful, who shamed the invasion army of 43 into embarking and engineered Messalina's fall; forced to suicide on Nero's accession.

people.name: Agrippina the Younger
people.summary: Daughter of Germanicus, sister of Caligula, fourth wife of Claudius and mother of Nero, whom she brought to the throne. The first living wife of an emperor called Augusta, she shared power openly in Nero's first years until he had her murdered.
people.detail: Her lost memoirs were a source for Tacitus and Pliny. She founded Cologne as a colony (Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium) in her birthplace in 50. Ancient tradition credits her with poisoning Claudius.
people.death: murdered on Nero's orders at Baiae, March 59

people.name: Britannicus
people.summary: Son of Claudius and Messalina, named for his father's British conquest, displaced by Nero's adoption and poisoned at dinner in 55, just before he turned fourteen.

people.name: Claudia Octavia
people.summary: Daughter of Claudius and Messalina, married to Nero in 53, divorced and murdered on Pandateria in 62 so that he could marry Poppaea; heroine of the tragedy Octavia.

people.name: Nero
people.fullName: Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus (born Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus)
people.summary: Last Julio-Claudian emperor, son of Agrippina the Younger. Guided early by Seneca and Burrus, he later murdered his mother, wives and rivals, performed publicly as singer and charioteer, rebuilt Rome after the fire of 64 and persecuted Christians. Revolts in Gaul and Spain and the desertion of the guard drove him to suicide.
people.detail: Popular with the urban plebs and in the Greek East (several 'false Neros' appeared after his death), he was execrated by the senatorial tradition. Champlin's Nero (2003) reads his conduct as calculated showmanship. Christian tradition made him the Antichrist.

people.name: Poppaea Sabina
people.summary: Wife of Otho, then mistress and (62) wife of Nero; Josephus calls her a 'God-fearer' sympathetic to Jews. She died pregnant, supposedly after Nero kicked her, and was deified.

people.name: Seneca
people.summary: Stoic philosopher, tragedian and statesman from Corduba, exiled to Corsica by Claudius (41-49), recalled by Agrippina to tutor Nero and co-director of government with Burrus until 62; forced to suicide after the Pisonian conspiracy.
people.detail: His works include the Moral Letters to Lucilius, dialogues (De ira, De clementia, De brevitate vitae), Natural Questions, nine tragedies and the satire Apocolocyntosis. His vast wealth (300 million sesterces) and loans in Britain sat uneasily with his preaching; critics such as Suillius Rufus attacked his hypocrisy.

people.name: Burrus
people.summary: Gallic equestrian from Vasio, praetorian prefect appointed through Agrippina, who with Seneca guided Nero's early government; his death in 62, perhaps by poison, removed a key restraint.

people.name: Tigellinus
people.summary: Nero's notorious praetorian prefect and organiser of his entertainments and repressions after 62, blamed for the second outbreak of the Great Fire; he abandoned Nero in 68 and was forced to suicide by Otho.

people.name: Corbulo
people.summary: The outstanding general of the mid-first century, famous for harsh discipline. He crushed the Chauci (47), conquered Armenia for Nero (58-60) and negotiated the Rhandeia settlement (63); Nero ordered him to die in 67.
people.detail: Tacitus's narrative of the Armenian war appears to draw on Corbulo's own memoirs. His daughter Domitia Longina married Domitian. His troops' exploits were remembered by the Flavian generals who had served under him.

people.name: Varus
people.summary: Senator related by marriage to Augustus, governor of Africa and Syria (where he crushed the revolt after Herod's death), whose attempt to impose Roman law and tribute in Germany ended in the destruction of three legions in AD 9.
people.detail: Velleius calls him a man of mild character, more suited to camp leisure than war, who 'came poor to rich Syria and left rich Syria poor'. Modern scholars see him more as the victim of an unworkable policy and of Arminius's betrayal.
people.death: suicide during the Varian disaster, September AD 9

people.name: Arminius

roles.t: Commander of Cheruscan auxiliaries in Roman service

people.summary: Cheruscan noble, Roman citizen and equestrian, who led the ambush that destroyed Varus's legions in AD 9, fought Germanicus to a standstill (15-16), defeated Maroboduus (17), and was murdered by his own kinsmen for aspiring to kingship.
people.detail: Tacitus calls him 'without doubt the liberator of Germany'. His wife Thusnelda, daughter of the pro-Roman Segestes, was captured and paraded in Germanicus's triumph with their son. From the sixteenth century he became 'Hermann', a German national hero, culminating in the Hermannsdenkmal near Detmold (1875).

people.name: Segestes
people.summary: Pro-Roman Cheruscan noble who warned Varus of Arminius's plot, was besieged by Arminius (who had abducted his daughter Thusnelda) and rescued by Germanicus in 15, and watched his daughter paraded in the triumph of 17.

people.name: Inguiomerus
people.summary: Uncle of Arminius and Cheruscan war-leader who pressed the attack on Caecina's camp at Pontes Longi (15), escaped from Idistaviso (16), and later defected to Maroboduus.

people.name: Maroboduus
people.summary: Roman-educated king who led the Marcomanni to Bohemia and built a powerful kingdom with an army of 70,000 foot and 4,000 horse; Rome's planned attack on him in AD 6 was aborted by the Illyrian revolt. Defeated by Arminius and expelled, he spent 18 years in exile at Ravenna.

people.name: Bato the Daesitiate

roles.t: Leader of the Great Illyrian Revolt

people.summary: Leader of the Dalmatian Daesitiates who began the Great Illyrian Revolt in AD 6, executed his Breucian namesake for treachery, and surrendered to Tiberius at Andetrium in 9, famously blaming Rome's 'wolves' for the rising. He was interned at Ravenna.
people.death: in comfortable internment at Ravenna, date unknown

people.name: Bato the Breucian
people.summary: Leader of the Pannonian Breuci in the Great Illyrian Revolt who betrayed his fellow leader Pinnes to the Romans in AD 8 and was then captured and executed by Bato the Daesitiate.

people.name: Caecina Severus
people.summary: Veteran commander who fought forty campaigns: he relieved Sirmium and fought at the Volcaean Marshes in the Illyrian revolt and led Germanicus's lower army, narrowly escaping at Pontes Longi (15).

people.name: Plautius Silvanus
people.summary: Consul of 2 BC, governor of Galatia, who brought eastern legions to the Illyrian war and fought at the Volcaean Marshes; his family tomb survives near Tibur.

people.name: Sentius Saturninus
people.summary: Consul of 19 BC who resisted Egnatius Rufus's candidacy, governed Syria, and commanded the Rhine army that was to strike Maroboduus from the west in AD 6.

people.name: Lucius Caedicius
people.summary: Camp prefect who held the fort of Aliso after the Varian disaster and led its garrison and civilians in a night breakout to the Rhine.

people.name: Nonius Asprenas
people.summary: Nephew of Varus whose two legions on the upper Rhine secured the river crossings after the disaster of AD 9 and prevented panic spreading to Gaul; accused of seizing the dead men's property.

people.name: Velleius Paterculus

roles.t: Cavalry prefect and legate under Tiberius

people.summary: Officer who served with Gaius Caesar in the East and Tiberius in Germany and Illyricum, and whose brief Roman history (published AD 30) is an eyewitness but adulatory source for Tiberius and Sejanus.

people.name: Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso
people.summary: Proud aristocrat appointed governor of Syria alongside Germanicus's eastern command, accused of poisoning him and of trying to recover his province by force; he killed himself during his trial, recorded in the senatus consultum de Cn. Pisone patre.

people.name: Plancina
people.summary: Wife of Gnaeus Piso and friend of Livia, suspected of poisoning Germanicus with the help of a notorious poisoner, Martina; pardoned at Livia's request in 20 but forced to suicide in 33.

people.name: Tacfarinas
people.summary: Numidian deserter from Roman auxiliary service who organised the Musulamii and Moorish tribes into units trained in Roman fashion and waged guerrilla war in Africa for seven years, until killed at Auzea.

people.name: Junius Blaesus
people.summary: Uncle of Sejanus who faced the Pannonian mutiny of 14 and fought Tacfarinas, becoming the last man outside the imperial family to be hailed imperator by his troops; he fell with his nephew.

people.name: Publius Cornelius Dolabella
people.summary: Proconsul of Africa who ended the war of Tacfarinas at Auzea in 24 but was refused triumphal ornaments to spare Sejanus's uncle Blaesus.

people.name: Gaius Silius
people.summary: Commander of the upper Rhine army who crushed Sacrovir's revolt in 21; prosecuted for treason in 24 as a friend of Germanicus's family, he killed himself. Father of Messalina's lover of the same name.

people.name: Julius Sacrovir
people.summary: Aeduan noble and Roman citizen who led the Gallic revolt of 21, seizing Augustodunum; defeated by Gaius Silius, he burned himself and his companions in a villa.

people.name: Seius Tubero
people.summary: Half-brother (or adoptive brother) of Sejanus who commanded the cavalry under Germanicus in 16 and was suffect consul in 18.

people.name: Poppaeus Sabinus
people.summary: Long-serving governor of Moesia, Achaea and Macedonia (24 years, Tacitus says, because he was 'equal to his tasks and no more'), who suppressed the Thracian revolt of 26; grandfather of Poppaea Sabina.

people.name: Lucius Apronius
people.summary: Commander who decimated a cowardly cohort in the war against Tacfarinas and later failed against the Frisian revolt of 28, losing 900 men at Baduhenna Wood.

people.name: Cremutius Cordus
people.summary: Historian of the civil wars and Augustus prosecuted in 25 for praising Brutus and Cassius; he starved himself and his books were burned, but his daughter Marcia saved copies.

people.name: Ptolemy of Mauretania
people.summary: Last king of Mauretania, son of Juba II and Cleopatra Selene and thus grandson of Antony and Cleopatra. He helped Rome defeat Tacfarinas but was killed by his cousin Caligula, and his kingdom was annexed.

people.name: Archelaus of Cappadocia
people.summary: Client king of Cappadocia for over fifty years, appointed by Antony, whose summons to Rome and death in 17 led Tiberius to annex his kingdom.

people.name: Rhoemetalces I
people.summary: Client king of Thrace whose cavalry fought for Rome in the Great Illyrian Revolt, notably at the Volcaean Marshes.

people.name: Phraates IV
people.summary: Arsacid king who defeated Antony (36 BC) and returned the Roman standards to Augustus in 20 BC; he sent four sons to Rome as hostages and was murdered by his wife Musa and son Phraataces.

people.name: Amyntas of Galatia
people.summary: Client king installed by Antony who deserted to Octavian before Actium; killed by the Homonadenses in 25 BC, after which his kingdom became the province of Galatia.

people.name: Herod the Great
people.summary: Idumaean-born client king of Judaea, installed by Rome in 40/37 BC, a loyal friend of Antony and then of Augustus and Agrippa. He was a prodigious builder (the Temple, Caesarea, Masada, Herodium, Machaerus) and a ruthless dynast who executed his wife Mariamme and three sons.

people.name: Quirinius
people.summary: New man from Lanuvium who subdued the Homonadenses, advised Gaius Caesar in the East, and as legate of Syria carried out the census of Judaea in AD 6 mentioned in Luke's Gospel.

people.name: Pontius Pilate
people.summary: Equestrian prefect of Judaea who provoked Jewish protests by bringing military standards into Jerusalem and using Temple funds for an aqueduct, ordered the crucifixion of Jesus, and was recalled after a massacre of Samaritans. A dedicatory inscription from Caesarea confirms his title.

people.name: Jesus of Nazareth
people.summary: Galilean Jewish teacher and healer proclaiming the kingdom of God, crucified in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate around 30 or 33; the movement of his followers became Christianity.

people.name: Paul of Tarsus
people.summary: Diaspora Jew and Roman citizen, persecutor turned apostle, whose missions in Asia Minor and Greece and whose letters, the earliest Christian documents, shaped Gentile Christianity. Tradition places his execution in Rome under Nero.

people.name: Peter the Apostle
people.summary: Galilean fisherman and leading disciple of Jesus, later a missionary; early tradition (1 Clement, Ignatius, Dionysius of Corinth) places his martyrdom in Rome under Nero, and his tomb was venerated on the Vatican hill.

people.name: Philo of Alexandria
people.summary: Jewish Platonist philosopher and exegete of Alexandria who led the Jewish embassy to Caligula in 39/40; his In Flaccum and Embassy to Gaius are eyewitness sources for the crisis of 38-41.

people.name: Agrippa I
people.summary: Grandson of Herod, raised in Rome with the imperial princes, friend of Caligula and Claudius; he dissuaded Caligula from desecrating the Temple, mediated Claudius's accession, and ruled all Herod's kingdom until his sudden death.

people.name: Agrippa II

roles.t: King of Chalcis and northern territories

people.summary: Son of Agrippa I, client king with authority over the Temple, who tried to prevent the revolt of 66, fought on the Roman side, and supplied Josephus with information. His sister Berenice was Titus's lover.

people.name: Publius Petronius
people.summary: Legate of Syria ordered by Caligula to set up the emperor's statue in the Jerusalem Temple; he delayed in the face of mass protest and was spared execution only by Caligula's death.

people.name: Aulus Plautius
people.summary: Commander of the Claudian invasion of Britain and its first governor, awarded the last ovatio granted to a non-imperial general (47). His wife Pomponia Graecina was tried for a 'foreign superstition', possibly Christianity.

people.name: Hosidius Geta
people.summary: Officer who campaigned against the Moors in 42 and won the second day of the Medway battle in 43, receiving triumphal ornaments before reaching the consulship.

people.name: Caratacus
people.summary: Son of Cunobelinus who led British resistance against Rome for eight years, from the Medway to Wales; betrayed by Cartimandua in 51 and pardoned by Claudius after his celebrated speech in Rome.

people.name: Togodumnus
people.summary: Brother of Caratacus and joint leader of British resistance in 43; he died shortly after the Romans crossed the Thames.
people.death: died of wounds or in battle, 43

people.name: Togidubnus

roles.t: Client king (rex magnus) in southern Britain

people.summary: British client king whom Tacitus says remained loyal 'down to our own times'; an inscription from Chichester (RIB 91) calls him 'great king of Britain'. The Fishbourne palace is often associated with him.

people.name: Ostorius Scapula
people.summary: Second governor of Britain, who disarmed the allied tribes (provoking an Icenian revolt), founded the colony at Camulodunum and defeated Caratacus, but died exhausted by the Silurian war.

people.name: Suetonius Paullinus
people.summary: First Roman to cross the Atlas mountains (42), conqueror of Mona and victor over Boudica (60/61); in 69 he advised Otho against giving battle at Bedriacum.

people.name: Boudica

roles.t: Queen and war-leader of the Iceni

people.summary: Widow of the Icenian client king Prasutagus who, after being flogged and her daughters raped by Roman officials, led the great revolt of 60/61 that destroyed Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium before her defeat by Suetonius Paullinus.
people.detail: Dio describes her as tall, with a harsh voice and a mass of tawny hair to her hips, wearing a great gold torc. Tacitus gives her a speech presenting her as avenging lost liberty and the outraged bodies of her daughters. She became a British national icon in the Victorian era (Thomas Thornycroft's statue on Westminster Bridge).
people.death: poison (Tacitus) or illness (Dio) after defeat, 60 or 61

people.name: Prasutagus
people.summary: Wealthy client king of the Iceni who left half his kingdom to Nero in the hope of protecting his family; Roman officials treated the kingdom as conquered, provoking his widow Boudica's revolt.

people.name: Cartimandua
people.summary: Pro-Roman queen of the Brigantes who handed Caratacus over to Rome in 51; after she replaced her husband Venutius with his armour-bearer, Venutius overthrew her in 69 and Rome evacuated her.

people.name: Julius Classicianus
people.summary: Gallic-born procurator sent to Britain after the Boudican revolt, who reported that Paullinus's reprisals were prolonging the war; his tombstone, found in London, is in the British Museum (RIB 12).

people.name: Quintus Veranius
people.summary: First governor of Lycia, whose road-building is recorded on the Stadiasmus Patarensis; he died in his first year as governor of Britain, boasting in his will that he would have conquered the island in two more years.

people.name: Gallio
people.summary: Elder brother of Seneca, proconsul of Achaea before whom Paul was accused at Corinth (Acts 18); the Delphi inscription naming him fixes Pauline chronology. He perished after the Pisonian conspiracy.

people.name: Cassius Longinus
people.summary: Leading jurist of the Sabinian school, descendant of the tyrannicide Cassius, who argued for executing Pedanius Secundus's 400 slaves in 61; exiled by Nero in 65 and recalled by Vespasian.

people.name: Gaius Calpurnius Piso
people.summary: Popular, generous aristocrat chosen by the conspirators of 65 as Nero's replacement; when the plot was betrayed he opened his veins, his will flattering Nero to protect his wife.

people.name: Lucan
people.summary: Nephew of Seneca and author of the epic Pharsalia (Bellum Civile) on the war of Caesar and Pompey; banned from publishing by a jealous Nero, he joined the Pisonian conspiracy and was forced to die aged 25, reciting his own verses.

people.name: Petronius
people.summary: Nero's 'arbiter of elegance', probably the author of the Satyricon. Denounced by Tigellinus, he slowly bled to death amid conversation and light verse, sending Nero a catalogue of the emperor's debaucheries.

people.name: Thrasea Paetus
people.summary: Stoic senator from Patavium whose silent opposition (walking out of the Senate after Agrippina's murder) made him the emblem of senatorial independence; condemned in 66, his death closes the surviving Annals.

people.name: Nymphidius Sabinus
people.summary: Praetorian prefect who detached the guard from Nero in June 68 by promising a huge donative in Galba's name, then tried to seize power himself and was killed by the praetorians.

people.name: Gessius Florus
people.summary: Procurator of Judaea whose extortion and seizure of Temple funds, followed by a massacre in Jerusalem, Josephus blames for provoking the revolt of 66.

people.name: Cestius Gallus
people.summary: Legate of Syria whose withdrawal from Jerusalem in 66 turned into the rout at Beth Horon; he died, 'by fate or weariness' says Tacitus, early in 67.

people.name: Caesennius Paetus
people.summary: General who capitulated to Vologases at Rhandeia in 62; pardoned with a joke by Nero, he later, as Vespasian's governor of Syria, annexed Commagene (72).

people.name: Tiridates I
people.summary: Brother of Vologases I and Zoroastrian magus, installed in Armenia by Parthia, driven out by Corbulo, and finally crowned by Nero in Rome in 66 under the Rhandeia compromise, founding the Arsacid dynasty of Armenia.

people.name: Vologases I
people.summary: Arsacid king who installed his brother Tiridates in Armenia, forced Paetus's capitulation at Rhandeia, accepted the compromise of 63, and later offered Vespasian 40,000 mounted archers in 69.

people.name: Antiochus IV of Commagene
people.summary: Richest of the client kings, restored to Commagene by Caligula, an ally in the Armenian and Jewish wars, deposed in 72 on a charge of plotting with Parthia; his grandson Philopappus became an Athenian archon and Roman consul.

people.name: Plautius Silvanus Aelianus
people.summary: Neronian legate of Moesia whose funerary inscription near Tibur (ILS 986) records his settling of over 100,000 Transdanubians in the province, intervention in the Crimea and grain shipments to Rome.

people.name: Virgil
people.summary: Poet from near Mantua, author of the Eclogues, Georgics and Aeneid, Rome's national epic, which made Aeneas's mission and Augustus's destiny one story; he died before completing the Aeneid.

people.name: Horace
people.summary: Freedman's son from Venusia who fought for Brutus at Philippi and became, through Maecenas, the lyric voice of the Augustan age (Odes, Epodes, Satires, Epistles, Ars Poetica) and composer of the Carmen Saeculare.

people.name: Ovid
people.summary: Equestrian poet from Sulmo, author of the Amores, Ars Amatoria, Metamorphoses and Fasti, relegated by Augustus to Tomis in AD 8 for 'a poem and a mistake'; he died in exile.

people.name: Aelius Gallus
people.summary: Second prefect of Egypt, friend of Strabo, who led the failed expedition to Arabia Felix in 26-25 BC.

people.name: Cornelius Gallus
people.summary: Elegiac poet and friend of Virgil, Octavian's general at the conquest of Egypt and its first prefect, whose self-glorifying inscriptions led to his disgrace and suicide.

people.name: Gaius Petronius
people.summary: Prefect of Egypt who repelled the Kushite invasion, sacked Napata (24 BC) and relieved Primis.

people.name: Amanirenas
people.summary: Kushite queen, probably the one-eyed 'Candace' of Strabo, who with prince Akinidad attacked Roman Egypt in 25 BC and secured favourable terms at Samos; the Meroë head of Augustus is a trophy of her war.

people.name: Publius Carisius
people.summary: Augustan legate who defeated the Astures and took Lancia (25 BC) and founded Augusta Emerita; his harshness provoked a renewed revolt.

people.name: Varro Murena
people.summary: Brother-in-law of Maecenas who destroyed the Salassi (25 BC) and is usually identified with the Murena executed for conspiracy in 23/22 BC.

people.name: Marcus Licinius Crassus (cos. 30 BC)
people.summary: Grandson of the triumvir who defeated the Bastarnae and Getae and killed king Deldo in single combat, but was denied the spolia opima; he triumphed in July 27 BC and then vanishes.

people.name: Marcus Lollius
people.summary: First governor of Galatia, defeated by the Sugambri in 16 BC with the loss of an eagle, later guardian of Gaius Caesar in the East, disgraced for taking bribes.

people.name: Maelo
people.summary: Sugambrian leader named in the Res Gestae (32) as a king who came to Augustus as a suppliant; probably a leader of the attack on Lollius in 16 BC.

people.name: Cornelius Balbus the Younger
people.summary: Native of Gades who conquered the Garamantes and celebrated the last triumph of a non-imperial Roman (19 BC); builder of the Theatre of Balbus.

people.name: Silius Nerva
people.summary: Governor of Illyricum who subdued the Camunni and Vennii and repelled Norican and Pannonian raiders in 16 BC, paving the way for the incorporation of Noricum.
